lessons.title: What Investors Look For at Seed vs Series A

children.text: Two founders pitch the same investor in the same week. The first has no revenue, a half-built product and a five-year plan on slide 14. She gets a cheque. The second has ₹2 crore of revenue, a full team and a working product. He gets a polite no. Nothing about that is unfair or random. The two were being judged against completely different questions, because a seed investor and a Series A investor are buying different things. This lesson shows you what each one is actually testing.

body.text: Seed investors buy a story that could be true. Series A investors buy proof that it already is. Between those two rounds, your job changes from convincing people to showing them data they cannot argue with.

children.text: The Same Five Boxes, Weighted Differently

Almost every investor, from an angel in Nagpur to a partner at a large Bengaluru fund, assesses the same five things: team, market, product, traction and economics. What changes between seed and Series A is how much weight each one carries and how much evidence is demanded.

body.caption: The same questions, asked very differently

cells: Team
Can these founders build it? Do they know this problem personally?
Can they hire and manage 60 people? Is there a leadership team, not just founders?
Market
Could this be very large if it works?
Is this market real and reachable, with a credible path to a few hundred crore of revenue?
Product
Does something work, and do early users like it?
Is it reliable at scale, and is the roadmap driven by customers rather than guesses?
Traction
Any real signal: paying users, repeat usage, a waiting list
Consistent growth over several quarters, with retention that holds up
Economics
Do the founders understand what a customer costs and earns?
Proven unit economics: acquisition cost pays back and the maths survives scale
Governance
Clean incorporation, clear founder split, no hidden liabilities
Audited financials, proper compliance, board-ready reporting and controls

columns.label: The seed investor's bet
points: Backs founders and a market, mostly on judgement
Expects the plan to change, sometimes completely
Accepts that most of the portfolio will fail
Decides in weeks, on conviction and references
Asks: is this team worth betting on before anyone else does?

columns.label: The Series A investor's bet
points: Backs evidence, verified in a data room
Expects the model to be stable enough to scale
Needs this company to be a potential fund returner
Decides in months, with diligence, references and an investment committee
Asks: if we pour ₹40 crore into this machine, does it hold?

children.text: At Seed, You Are the Evidence

With little data to analyse, a seed investor falls back on three questions. Why this problem, why now, and why you. The third is where most Indian seed rounds are won or lost. Founder-market fit, meaning a real reason you understand this problem better than the next team, beats a polished deck every time. A founder whose family ran a pharmacy distribution business has an unfair advantage pitching pharmacy software, and every good seed investor knows it.

body.label: The question behind "why now"
body.value: What changed in the last 24 months that makes this possible today?
body.context: UPI reaching small merchants, cheap cloud, ONDC, GST data, falling smartphone costs, a new SEBI or RBI rule: a credible seed pitch names the shift that opened the window, because a good idea with no timing trigger usually means someone already tried it and failed.

body.title: What kills this seed pitch?
body.question: Two ex-bankers pitch a lending app for gig workers. The deck has a ₹90,000 crore market size, a clean product design, a 5-year projection ending at ₹800 crore of revenue, and a slide saying they will hire a credit head after the round. What is a seed investor's biggest concern?
options: The market size is too small to matter
Nobody on the founding team has built or run a lending book, which is the core risk of the business
The five-year projection is not detailed enough
The product design needs more work before any investor commits
body.explanation: At seed, the team is the product. Lending lives or dies on credit underwriting and collections, and the founders plan to hire that expertise later, after taking the money. Investors know five-year projections are fiction at this stage, so they test whether this specific team can survive the hardest part of this specific business.

children.text: At Series A, the Data Is the Evidence

markDefs.definition: A growth engine is repeatable when a known amount of spend or effort in a known channel reliably produces a known number of customers, month after month.

children.text: A Series A investor is not looking for a bigger version of your seed pitch. They are looking for

. One brilliant quarter proves nothing. Six months of consistent growth in the same channel, with customers who stay, proves that money can be poured in at one end and growth reliably comes out the other. Chapter 5 returns to this, and Lesson 2.2 covers the metrics themselves in detail.

body.title: Two startups, eight quarters (revenue, ₹ crore annualised)

body.text: Startup B was ahead for four quarters and is still bigger than A was a year ago. It will struggle to raise a Series A anyway. Investors price the slope, not the level. A smaller company growing 3 times a year is far more fundable than a larger one that has flattened, because the slope is what a ₹40 crore cheque is supposed to multiply.

stats.label: Growth
stats.context: The common Series A ambition, sustained rather than one good quarter

stats.label: Consistency
stats.context: Enough data points that the trend cannot be explained by one big customer

stats.label: Retention
stats.value: Customers still there a year later
stats.context: Growth on top of churn is a leaking bucket, and diligence finds it

stats.label: Unit economics
stats.context: Usually within about a year, and faster is better in Indian consumer businesses

body.title: Measure the slope
body.prompt: A Pune SaaS company grew from ₹1.2 crore of annual recurring revenue to ₹4.2 crore over twelve months. By what multiple did it grow in the year?
body.explanation: ₹4.2 crore ÷ ₹1.2 crore = 3.5 times. That is comfortably in Series A territory on growth alone. Investors will then check whether the growth came from many customers or one large contract, and whether last year's customers are still paying.

body.title: How a VC fund actually says yes

children.text: Founders often imagine one person deciding. In an institutional fund, a Series A usually travels through five gates, and each has a different failure mode.
The first meeting, often with an associate or principal. They are screening, not deciding.
A partner takes interest and becomes your champion inside the firm. Without one, nothing moves.
Deep diligence: cohort data, customer calls, founder references, financials and compliance.
The partnership or investment committee meeting, where your champion argues the case and others attack it.
A term sheet, then confirmatory diligence and definitive agreements, covered in Chapter 4.

Two practical consequences. First, identify early whether the person across the table can champion a deal internally, because meetings that never reach a partner cost you months. Second, your job is to make the champion's argument easy: clean data, consistent numbers and answers that hold up when you are not in the room.

body.caption: Common reasons behind a polite no

cells: "It is too early for us"
Your evidence does not match their stage, or the growth is not convincing yet
Ask what specific milestone would make it interesting, then go and hit it
"We are not sure about the market size"
They cannot see how this reaches a few hundred crore of revenue
Show a bottom-up market build, not a top-down report number
"Let us stay in touch and track progress"
A no for now, with an open door if the numbers improve
Send a short monthly update. Many rounds are won this way six months later
"We have a portfolio conflict"
Usually literally true, and nothing to do with your quality
Ask for an introduction to a fund without that conflict
Silence after diligence
Something in the data room did not reconcile, or a reference call went badly
Ask directly for the reason. Fix it before the next investor finds the same thing

body.text: Governance is now an early filter, not a closing formality. After several well-publicised failures at Indian startups involving overstated revenue, related-party transactions and delayed audits, investors check financial hygiene long before the term sheet. Unsigned board minutes, unfiled returns, cash sales with no trail or revenue recognised before delivery can end a process that was going well.

body.title: Which one gets the Series A?
body.scenario:
A fund can back only one of two Bengaluru companies, each raising ₹30 crore.
Company P: ₹6 crore annual recurring revenue, grew 3.2 times last year, 140 customers, none more than 6% of revenue, customers from last year still spending slightly more this year, acquisition cost pays back in 9 months, founders are ex-operators from the same industry, audited accounts and clean compliance.
Company Q: ₹11 crore revenue, grew 1.4 times last year, 9 customers, the largest is 48% of revenue, two customers left last year, acquisition is mostly founder-led sales, accounts unaudited for the latest year, and a related-party vendor owned by a co-founder's family.
body.prompt: Which company gets the term sheet, and what would you tell the other founder to fix?
body.modelAnswer:
Company P, despite being smaller.
Why P wins: 3.2 times growth, no customer concentration, customers expanding rather than churning, and acquisition cost paying back in 9 months. That is a repeatable machine, which is exactly what Series A money is meant to scale. Clean audits and compliance mean diligence will not derail.
Why Q loses: 1.4 times growth is not a venture trajectory, 48% concentration in one customer means one email can halve the business, founder-led sales is not a channel that scales with money, and the unaudited accounts plus a related-party vendor will dominate diligence instead of the business.
What Q should do: stop raising for two or three quarters. Get the accounts audited, disclose and clean up the related-party arrangement, bring the largest customer below about 20% of revenue by adding accounts, and build one repeatable sales channel that is not the founder. Then return with four quarters of evidence. Raising now means either no term sheet or a bad one signed from weakness.

body.title: Series A readiness self-check
steps: Can you show at least six months of consistent growth in the same chart, without explaining away any month?
Is any single customer more than about 20% of revenue?
Are customers from a year ago still buying, and can you prove it with cohort data?
Do you know what a customer costs to acquire and how long the payback takes?
Is there one growth channel that works without a founder personally closing every deal?
Are the last two years audited, with GST, TDS, ROC and ESOP paperwork in order?
Have you named the leadership hires the round will fund, and can you defend why those roles?

body.title: The word that decides a Series A
body.textWithBlank: A Series A investor is not paying for one good quarter. They are paying for ___, meaning a known input reliably produces a known amount of growth month after month.
body.explanation: Repeatability is what separates a seed story from a Series A case. It is why investors want several quarters of consistent data from the same channel, not a single spike.

cards.definition: A credible reason this specific team understands this specific problem better than others, which carries heavy weight at seed.
The recent change in technology, regulation or behaviour that makes the idea possible today when it was not before.
A known amount of spend or effort in a known channel producing a predictable number of customers, month after month.
The share of revenue coming from the largest customers. High concentration is a major Series A risk flag.
The partner inside a fund who argues for your deal internally. Without one, a process rarely progresses.
The forum where a fund's partners test and approve a deal before a term sheet is issued.

points: Seed and Series A investors assess the same five areas, team, market, product, traction and economics, but demand very different evidence.
At seed you are the evidence: founder-market fit, a credible why now, and a market that could become very large.
At Series A the data is the evidence: consistent growth over several quarters, retention that holds, and unit economics that survive scale.
Investors price the slope, not the level. A smaller company growing 3 times a year beats a larger one that has flattened.
A Series A moves through an internal process, so you need a partner willing to champion the deal, not just a good first meeting.
Governance is an early filter now. Unaudited accounts, related-party dealings and customer concentration end processes quietly.
Treat every no as data. Ask what milestone would change the answer, then send monthly updates and come back with it.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, legal or financial advice. Growth, retention and payback expectations are common market observations that vary by sector and funding conditions, not fixed standards. Companies P and Q and the other examples are illustrative. Speak to a qualified professional before making funding decisions for your company.
